chat.text: Create a conflict-free schedule. Start with an S-Bahn line running every 30 minutes. To do this, place one commuter rail token on position I and one in the opposite direction on position II
Note: We are not yet planning long-distance or freight service in this step. Please use only commuter rail tokens.
Not yet - the S-Bahn line starts with a 30-minute headway. Please rotate the commuter tokens back to 30 minutes.
Perfect – your schedule runs without conflicts. But what about the energy balance?
Still missing: one commuter token on position I and one on position II, both set to 30 minutes.
Press the “Energy Check” button
The result confirms your plan, but the simulation is very time-consuming. By purchasing the Energy feature, you can avoid unnecessary wait times and costs
Now plan an additional long-distance line on the A→C route, leaving the S-Bahn tokens in their positions.
Stop: Freight service should not be planned at this point yet; please use the long-distance tokens.
Not yet - leave the S-Bahn at its 30-minute headway for now, you will shorten it in a later step.
Then place the long-distance token at position IV – now the route is no longer conflict-free, because ETCS is missing on this section, making it unsuitable for long-distance service.
Try the long-distance token in another position.

faults.hint: No ETCS here - move the long-distance train to position III.

chat.text: The result: Long-distance service operates without conflicts only at position III, but you have to figure this out laboriously and time-consumingly through trial and error
Place the long-distance token on one of the two free positions on the A→C route.
Check the result using the Energy Check button. For position II, the result is OK; for position IV as well – so the schedule would work electrically, but not for operational reasons (no ETCS!).
Unfortunately, the feedback is unspecific (works/doesn’t work), and without the energy feature, waiting times and unnecessary costs arise again.
Now shorten the headway of the S-Bahn line from 30 to 20 minutes (by rotating the tokens)
Almost - both commuter tokens have to be set to 20 minutes.
Rotate both commuter tokens from 30 to 20 minutes.
The route coloring shows that your schedule is no longer energy-compatible.
Now try to resolve the conflict by adjusting or rotating the tokens.
Well done, but trial-and-error on both the S-Bahn headway and long-distance train operating status simultaneously means maximum effort, which is also reflected in the costs.
The commuter line has to keep its 20-minute headway - so it is the long-distance departure that has to move. Try rotating the token on position III.

faults.hint: Departure needs to be shifted by + 15 minutes.

chat.text: Now press the Energy Check button – this also takes a while. The result shows that your schedule works from an energy perspective, but in this configuration, you’ve incurred the highest costs.
Now plan an additional freight train on the A→C route by placing the freight traffic token on position IV.
The freight train belongs on position IV - position III stays with the long-distance line.
Place the freight token on position IV and leave the other tokens where they are.
Press the “Energy Check” button
The Energy Check shows that your schedule doesn’t work right away. Optimize your settings and check your schedule each time using the Energy Check button.
The two departures are still in each other’s way - rotate the long-distance and the freight token to different departure times.

faults.hint: Departure needs to be shifted by + 20 minutes.
Departure needs to be shifted by + 30 minutes.

chat.text: Press the “Energy Check” button
The final Energy Check also results in high costs and a significant time investment. However, you now have an energy-validated schedule that works.
A battery-powered train is supposed to run on an existing route – but the train’s range isn’t sufficient! Find a solution that optimally balances all four aspects of operational optimization.

Use the tokens to adjust the parameters:
- Battery token: Change battery capacity by rotating
- Schedule token: Change maximum speed by rotating
- Charging infrastructure token: Change route length by rotating, change location by moving
Find the optimal combination of all three tokens; the display of the four aspects of operational optimization will help you strike the right balance.
You’ve done it – you’ve found the optimal interplay between vehicles, infrastructure, and the schedule for the most efficient and cost-effective operation of the battery-powered train.

Possible solutions: Set the battery and infrastructure tokens to “maximum”: Now there is enough energy for operation, but your costs skyrocket; route utilization is optimal, and the number of trains required is low.
Reduce the travel speed and improve the charging infrastructure; even then, there is enough energy, but more trains are needed and costs rise moderately, while route utilization improves.
If you set the schedule token to “slow operation” and the battery token to “high capacity,” your vehicle costs will increase with moderate route utilization and additional vehicle requirements.
Set different battery capacities on the battery token: Even at the maximum possible battery capacity, the route is too long; the train would come to a standstill, and operation is not possible.

If you place the charging infrastructure token in the middle of the route and set it to maximum supply length, there is still not enough energy. At the same time, the four aspects of operational optimization change: high infrastructure costs, low vehicle costs, low route utilization, and few trains required, but as a result, the schedule cannot be implemented.

If you set the schedule token to slow speed, the range is still too short and the train would take too long. This reduces route utilization, and costs remain moderate, but more trains would have to be deployed to maintain the frequency.

kpis.name: Operational utilization of the rail network

chat.text: Plan a traction power supply that will allow you to implement an existing schedule. Determine how many substations you’ll need for this.
A new schedule is now available. It’s clear that it cannot be implemented with the existing traction power supply. Will you adjust your traction power supply to implement the new schedule?
To do this, first load the new schedule into the system. Doing this manually is a time-consuming process that ties up a lot of resources.

After loading the new schedule, you’ll see that the traction power supply is insufficient to implement it. To change this, you can either relocate the substations or change their type (1AC, 2AC, SFC) by rotating the tokens.
Now the schedule has changed (again). As soon as the new schedule is loaded, you’ll see whether it can be implemented with the existing traction power settings.

Load the new schedule. If you had previously configured only 1AC substations, the entire rail network will not have sufficient power for the new schedule. If you had configured 2AC, the area without a substation will appear as faulty. However, if you use an SFC instead, the schedule can be implemented.
Adjust your traction power supply, either by adding more 2AC substations or by using more powerful SFC substations.
Load the new schedule. If you have used only 2AC substations, your traction power supply will no longer be sufficient at locations where there is no substation to implement the new schedule.
The schedule import is faster using the TPS/Sidytrac Import-Export function. Place an SFC substation on the vacant position,
